C5M.1.q: You turn up a macro that has no slots set. What happens to the sound?
options: The filter opens, as that is its usual job
The note gets louder as the macro rises
Nothing: a macro does nothing by itself
Every knob on the synth moves a little
C5M.1.why: A macro only moves the knobs its slots point to, so with no slots it changes nothing.

C5M.1.q: How many slots can you give one macro?
options: Only one
Up to three
Exactly two
As many as there are knobs
C5M.1.why: A macro takes up to three slots, and each slot moves a knob of its own.

C5M.1.q: You set a slot to Cutoff with an amount, but the macro is still at zero. What changes in the sound?
options: Nothing yet: the slot only says what the macro will do
The filter opens at once by the slot's amount
The filter closes until the macro is turned up
The note stops until the macro has been named
C5M.1.why: A slot is a destination and an amount; nothing moves until the macro itself is turned.

C5M.1.q: You set slot 1 to Cutoff. A faint ring appears on the Cutoff knob. What does it show?
options: How far the macro has been turned so far
How loud the filter is at this moment
That the knob can no longer be turned by hand
How far the macro can take that knob
C5M.1.why: The faint ring on a destination knob shows how far the macro can take it.

C5M.1.q: Cutoff and Resonance are both on one macro. What do you hear as you turn it up?
options: The filter opens first, then the edge sharpens later
The note gets louder but keeps the same tone
The filter opens and the edge sharpens together
Nothing, until you also turn both knobs by hand
C5M.1.why: Every slot moves together, so the filter opens and the resonance rises in the same motion.

C5M.1.q: Your bass needs more bite while you are playing. With the Bite macro built, what do you reach for?
options: Cutoff first, then Resonance, one after the other
The one macro knob, which moves the two together
The name box, to type in a stronger name
Slot 1's amount, to raise it as you play
C5M.1.why: A macro is for performance: you reach for one knob in place of two.

C5M.1.q: Which is the best kind of name for this macro?
options: One that lists the wiring, such as Cutoff and Resonance
One that gives its number, such as Macro 1
One that gives its amounts, so they can be read
One that says what it does to the sound, such as Bite
C5M.1.why: A macro is named for what it does to the sound, which helps when a patch has several.

C5M.2.q: A slot sends the macro to Osc A level with a negative amount. What happens to A as the macro rises?
options: It gets louder
It gets quieter
It stays at the same level
It changes from a saw to a square
C5M.2.why: A negative amount turns its knob down as the macro goes up.

C5M.2.q: Oscillator B starts silent, and the macro fades from A to B. What do you hear with the macro in the middle?
options: A blend of the saw and the square
Only the saw, as at the start
Only the hollow square
Silence, because the two cancel out
C5M.2.why: The middle of a crossfade macro is a mix of both layers.

C5M.2.q: You turn the Morph macro right up while watching the spectrum. What happens as B takes over?
options: Every peak grows taller
Every peak slides to the right
Every other peak drops out
Only the lowest peak is left
C5M.2.why: As the saw fades into the hollow square, every other peak drops out of the spectrum.

C5M.2.q: A dirty layer starts silent. You want one macro to fade from the clean layer to it. Which slot amounts?
options: Clean level negative, dirty level positive
Clean level positive, dirty level negative
Each level positive, by the same amount
Each level negative, by the same amount
C5M.2.why: The macro must take the clean layer down while it brings the silent dirty layer up.

C5M.3.q: In the brightness macro, what does the wavetable position slot change?
options: Which harmonics get through the filter
Which harmonics exist to begin with
How many new harmonics are added by squashing
How loud the whole sound is
C5M.3.why: The wavetable position decides which harmonics exist before the filter chooses what gets through.

C5M.3.q: You want the Bright macro to add new harmonics as it rises. Which slot does that?
options: The Cutoff slot
The Position slot
The Drive slot
The name of the macro
C5M.3.why: Drive adds new harmonics, while the filter and the wavetable position work on the ones already there.

C5M.3.q: Which is the better way to build a brightness macro?
options: A large amount on a single knob
Large amounts on every knob there is
Small amounts on several knobs
The very same amount on every slot
C5M.3.why: Several small moves add up to one musical gesture, which beats one large move.

C5M.3.q: How can you tell the brightness macro has turned out well?
options: It sounds like the instrument itself getting brighter
You can pick out each of the three knobs moving
It sounds like a single filter knob being turned
The tone stays dull while the level rises
C5M.3.why: The three slots should be heard as one change, not three separate ones.

C5M.4.q: You want a macro that makes one voice sound bigger. Which two destinations do the widening?
options: Detune and Osc A level
Spread and Osc A level
Osc A level and Hold
Detune and Spread
C5M.4.why: Detune and spread do the two jobs for width, and the level slot works against them.

C5M.4.q: Why can turning up detune and spread be a problem in a mix?
options: Wider sounds are always quieter, so the part gets lost in it
Detune puts the note out of tune with the track
Spread removes the low end, so the sound thins
Bigger tends to be heard as louder, so the level jumps
C5M.4.why: Detuned, spread-out unison sounds bigger, and bigger tends to be heard as louder.

C5M.4.q: The Wide macro's third slot is Osc A level at a small negative amount. What does it do as the macro rises?
options: Turns the sound up a little so the width is noticed
Turns the sound down a little so the meter stays roughly put
Fades oscillator A out so only the unison remains
Narrows the sound again so it never gets too wide
C5M.4.why: A small negative level slot offsets the extra loudness that width brings.

C5M.4.q: What is the general job of a compensating slot in a macro?
options: To work against a side effect of the other slots
To double what the other slots already do
To switch the other slots off at the top
To keep the macro at zero until it is named
C5M.4.why: One slot can compensate for what the others do, which makes the macro nicer to play.

C5M.5.q: You want one knob to bring in an LFO's movement. Where can a macro's slot be sent?
options: Only to a knob that is part of the sound
To a setting of the LFO itself, such as its amount
Only to the cutoff that the LFO is moving
To the macro's own name, so it starts when named
C5M.5.why: A macro's destination can be a setting of an LFO or an envelope, not only part of the sound.

C5M.5.q: LFO 1 is already sent to the cutoff, but with an amount of zero. Why set it up that way?
options: So the LFO is switched off and can never be heard
So the wobble starts fast and slows down by itself
So nothing moves until the macro brings the wobble in
So the cutoff stays fully open the whole time
C5M.5.why: Starting the amount at zero keeps the bass still and lets the macro bring the movement in.

C5M.5.q: Your Wobble macro makes the wobble deeper as it rises, but never faster. Which slot is missing?
options: LFO 1 amount
Cutoff
Hold
LFO 1 rate
C5M.5.why: The amount slot brings the wobble in and the rate slot is the one that speeds it up.

C5M.5.q: Why does the Wobble macro feel like a build-up as you turn it?
options: The wobble gets deeper but slower at the same time
The note gets higher in pitch as it turns
The wobble keeps its depth while the note gets louder
The wobble gets deeper and faster at the same time
C5M.5.why: Depth and speed rising together is heard as growing intensity.

C5M.6.q: Which set of envelope moves takes a short pluck towards a slow pad?
options: Shorter attack, lower sustain, shorter release
Longer attack, lower sustain, shorter release
Shorter attack, higher sustain, shorter release
Longer attack, higher sustain, longer release
C5M.6.why: The macro travels from pluck to pad by lengthening attack and release and raising sustain.

C5M.6.q: What do struck notes sound like at the two ends of the Length macro?
options: Short plucks at the bottom, swelling pads at the top
Swelling pads at the bottom, short plucks at the top
Quiet notes at the bottom, loud notes at the top
Dull notes at the bottom, bright notes at the top
C5M.6.why: One knob turns one kind of instrument into another: plucks at the bottom, pads at the top.

C5M.6.q: You park the Length macro in the middle and strike a key. What do you hear?
options: The same short pluck as at the very bottom
The same full swelling pad as at the very top
Something in between a short pluck and a swelling pad
Nothing, until the macro is moved to one end
C5M.6.why: The macro travels between the pluck and the pad, so the middle gives a sound in between.

C5M.6.q: You turn the Length macro while a note is already sounding and hear no change. Why?
options: A macro cannot be sent to envelope settings
Envelope settings are read when a note starts
The macro only works while Hold is switched on
Envelope changes need the macro at full first
C5M.6.why: Envelope settings are read at the start of a note, so the change is heard on the next one.

C5M.7.q: In the Dirt macro, what does the noise layer add to the sound?
options: It squashes the shape of the wave
It adds a hard edge at the cutoff
It fills the gaps between the harmonics
It lowers the pitch of the note
C5M.7.why: Noise fills the gaps between the harmonics, which is heard as hiss.

C5M.7.q: You want the Dirt macro to add more hard edge at the cutoff. Which slot's amount do you raise?
options: The Resonance slot
The Drive slot
The Noise level slot
The slot with the largest amount
C5M.7.why: Resonance is the ingredient that adds a hard edge at the cutoff.

C5M.7.q: The noise oscillator is switched on but turned right down. Why?
options: So it waits in silence until the macro brings it in
So it can never be heard in this patch
So the drive has less signal to work on
So the filter stays closed while the macro rises
C5M.7.why: A source can sit silent until a macro raises its level.

C5M.7.q: The Dirt macro goes from clean to filthy by degrees. How should you use that?
options: Always turn it right up for the real effect
Stop wherever the sound is dirty enough
Leave it at zero and turn the three knobs
Jump between zero and full, never in between
C5M.7.why: By degrees is the point: you can stop where the sound is dirty enough.

C5M.8.q: How should the jobs be shared out between a finished patch's macros?
options: Each macro moves exactly one knob
Every macro does the same thing as a spare
Each macro stands for one musical idea
One macro does everything and the rest stay empty
C5M.8.why: A finished patch usually has several macros, each for one musical idea.

C5M.8.q: Bright is turned up and Wobble is left at zero. What do you hear?
options: A dark note that wobbles
A bright note that wobbles
The same dull, still note as before
A brighter note that stays still
C5M.8.why: The two macros are independent, so Bright alone brightens the note and adds no wobble.

C5M.8.q: You try Bright and Wobble at lots of different settings. What do you find?
options: Only four sounds: each macro on or off
Turning one macro up turns the other one down
Only the macro you turned last is heard
Every combination of the two is a different sound
C5M.8.why: The two macros are independent, so every combination of them is a different sound.

C5M.8.q: Both macros now reach the Cutoff knob. What happens there?
options: Only the first macro you connected counts
Their pushes add together
Only the larger of the two pushes counts
The two pushes cancel and Cutoff stays still
C5M.8.why: Two macros on one knob add together, just as two LFOs on one knob did.

C5M.8.q: Cutoff is now reached by Bright, Wobble and the LFO. What does the knob wear?
options: One ring, for whichever was connected last
One ring, for the largest push only
No rings, as three are too many to draw
A ring from each macro and one from the LFO
C5M.8.why: A knob wears a ring for each thing that reaches it, so every push can be seen.

C5M.8.q: You give Wobble a third slot: Cutoff, with a small negative amount. What do you hear as the wobble comes in?
options: The filter opens a little, so the wobble gets a brighter tone
The filter closes a little, so the wobble digs into a darker tone
The wobble stops, because the two macros cancel out
The wobble speeds up while the tone stays the same
C5M.8.why: A negative amount on Cutoff closes the filter a little as Wobble rises, giving a darker tone.

C5M.9.q: What goes amiss if you turn up only the reverb's size and not its level?
options: You get a huge hall you can barely hear
You get a tiny room that swamps the sound
You get a long train of separate echoes
You get a sound that is drier than before
C5M.9.why: Size and level usually want to move together, or the result is odd.

C5M.9.q: Which reverb makes a sound seem far away?
options: A little of a small room
A little of a big room
A lot of a big room
No reverb at all
C5M.9.why: A little of a small room is heard as close; a lot of a big room as far.

C5M.9.q: How does the sound seem with the Space macro at zero?
options: Quiet and at the back of a hall
Loud and inside a tiny room
Followed by a long, fading tail
Dry and right in front of you
C5M.9.why: The reverb starts at zero mix, so the sound is dry until the macro brings it in.

C5M.9.q: You turn the Space macro up in stages, striking a key each time. What do you hear?
options: A long tail shrinking to a short bloom, then dry
A pluck getting louder but staying completely dry
A dry pluck gaining a short bloom, then a long tail
A pluck followed by a train of separate repeats
C5M.9.why: As the room gets bigger and louder, the dry pluck gains a short bloom and then a long tail.

C5M.10.q: Why keep the delay silent most of the time?
options: A delay left on slowly drifts out of time
A delay left on all the time clutters a busy part
A delay left on makes every note quieter
A delay left on wears out its feedback
C5M.10.why: Keeping the delay silent and opening it for one moment avoids cluttering a busy part.

C5M.10.q: Why does the Throw macro raise feedback as well as the echo level?
options: So the echoes come closer together in time
So the first echo is louder than the note
So the echoes stop the moment you let go
So the echoes carry on in a long train
C5M.10.why: A throw needs the echoes turned up and enough feedback for them to keep going.

C5M.10.q: You want only the last note of a phrase to echo away. What do you do with the Throw macro?
options: Leave it turned up for the whole phrase
Turn it up once the phrase has ended
Turn it down on that note, then back up
Flick it up on that note, then bring it back down
C5M.10.why: The delay stays silent until you flick the macro up on the one note you want to throw.

C5M.10.q: You throw one note, then bring the macro back down. What happens to the echoes?
options: The tail dies away naturally
They repeat until you play another note
They get louder with each repeat
They jump back in on the next note
C5M.10.why: Bringing the macro down lets the echo tail fade out by itself.

C5M.11.q: What happens to the top end when distortion is pushed a long way?
options: It disappears completely
It becomes smooth and round
It turns to fizz
It drops down an octave
C5M.11.why: Distortion adds harmonics all the way up, and past a point the top turns to fizz.

C5M.11.q: Why is the EQ able to tame the distortion's harshness?
options: It comes after the distortion in the rack
It comes before the distortion in the rack
It is louder than the distortion
It swaps places with the distortion as the macro turns
C5M.11.why: Order matters: the EQ can only turn down highs that the distortion has already added.

C5M.11.q: The Heat macro's second slot is EQ high with a negative amount. What does that do?
options: Adds more and more top as the drive goes up
Rounds off more top as the drive goes up
Turns the drive down as the macro rises
Cuts the bass so the growl sounds thinner
C5M.11.why: The macro applies the cure in step with the cause: more heat, more of the top rounded off.

C5M.11.q: You turn the Heat macro up on a clean bass. What do you hear?
options: It thins into a bright buzz with a fizzy top
It gets quieter and duller, with no growl at all
It thickens into a warm, heavy growl without a harsh top
It stays clean while only the top end gets louder
C5M.11.why: Drive goes up and the high band comes down together, so the growl stays warm and not harsh.

C5M.12.q: Why is a macro a natural home for the sync sweep?
options: The sweep only sounds right when left in one place
The sweep is played by hand, not set and left
The sweep needs three slots to work at all
The sweep is too quiet without a macro's help
C5M.12.why: A sync sweep is played, so it suits one knob you turn by hand.

C5M.12.q: You build the Tear macro with only the Warp amount slot. What is the sweep like?
options: Thin at the bottom and piercing at the top
Dark at the bottom and dark at the top
Piercing at the bottom and thin at the top
Silent until a Cutoff slot is added
C5M.12.why: On its own the sync sweep can be thin at the bottom and piercing at the top.

C5M.12.q: Why does the Tear macro open the filter along with the sync sweep?
options: To keep the top of the sweep dark and the bottom bright
To make the sweep louder without changing its tone
To stop the sweep before it reaches the top
To keep the bottom of the sweep dark and let the top through later
C5M.12.why: The filter slot shapes how the sweep opens: dark low down, bright only when it gets there.

C5M.12.q: Why reach for a macro, not an LFO or envelope, to move the warp amount?
options: A macro moves a control faster than any source can
A source can only ever move the filter's cutoff
A macro can move a control that sources cannot reach
A source would move the cutoff slot the opposite way
C5M.12.why: Warp amount belongs on a macro, which is the way to move a control that sources cannot reach.

C5M.12.q: You turn the finished Tear macro slowly up and back down. What do you hear?
options: A bright scream sinking into a dark saw, then silence
A dark saw tearing open into a bright scream, then closing
A dark saw getting louder with no change in tone
A dark saw wobbling faster and faster, then stopping
C5M.12.why: The warp and the filter rise together, so a dark saw tears open into a bright, vowel-like scream.

C5M.13.q: What turns FM into a growl?
options: The FM amount keeps changing, so the tone snarls and relaxes
The FM amount stays fixed at its highest setting
The note's pitch keeps sliding up and down
The filter keeps opening and closing
C5M.13.why: A growl is FM whose amount keeps moving.

C5M.13.q: Which three things does the Growl macro raise together?
options: The FM, the cutoff and the resonance
The LFO's rate, the drive and the noise level
The FM, the LFO's amount and the LFO's rate
The FM, the detune and the spread
C5M.13.why: One macro raises the effect, how far it moves and how fast it moves.

C5M.13.q: Your growl has plenty of FM, but the tone barely snarls and relaxes. Which slot's amount do you raise?
options: The LFO 1 amount slot
The FM from B slot
The LFO 1 rate slot
The slot that was set up first
C5M.13.why: LFO 1's amount sets how far the LFO swings the FM, which is what makes the tone snarl and relax.

C5M.13.q: LFO 1 is already sent to FM from B, yet nothing moves with the macro at zero. Why?
options: The LFO only runs while the macro is being turned
The LFO's amount starts at zero until the macro raises it
Oscillator B is switched off until the macro is full
The LFO's rate is too fast to be heard
C5M.13.why: Starting the LFO's amount at zero leaves a plain sine and lets the macro bring the motion in.

C5M.13.q: You turn the Growl macro slowly up from zero. In what order does the sound change?
options: A snarl, then an edge, then a pure sine
A pure sine, then a louder sine, then silence
An edge, then a pure sine, then a slow fade
A pure sine, then an edge, then a snarl
C5M.13.why: The pure low sine grows an edge and then starts to snarl, faster and deeper as the macro rises.

C5M.14.q: When compressing harder, why lower the threshold?
options: So the signal is held more firmly
So the result ends up louder
So less of the signal is caught
So more of the signal is caught
C5M.14.why: A lower threshold catches more of the signal; the ratio decides how firmly it is held.

C5M.14.q: Your Squash macro catches plenty of the signal but does not hold it firmly. Which slot's amount do you raise?
options: The Compressor threshold slot
The Compressor ratio slot
The Compressor make-up slot
The slot with the negative amount
C5M.14.why: Raising the ratio is the move that holds the caught signal more firmly.

C5M.14.q: What happens if the macro lowers the threshold and raises the ratio but adds no make-up gain?
options: The sound just shrinks
The sound gets louder and louder
Soft and hard notes move further apart
The compressor stops doing anything
C5M.14.why: Compression leaves the result quieter, so make-up gain is the slot that keeps the level.

C5M.14.q: With the Squash macro at zero, how do soft and hard notes compare?
options: Nearly the same level, because the compressor is working
Both silent, because the compressor is switched off
Far apart in level, because the compressor does nothing
Both at full level, because make-up is at its highest
C5M.14.why: At zero the compressor is in the path but doing nothing, so soft and hard notes stay apart.

C5M.14.q: You turn the Squash macro up in stages, striking keys. What does the “Turning down by” reading do?
options: It shrinks as the macro rises
It stays at nothing the whole way
It grows as the macro rises
It jumps about with no pattern
C5M.14.why: The harder the macro makes the compressor work, the more the reading grows.

C5M.15.q: Which three changes make up the Shimmer macro?
options: Reverb fading in, getting larger, and a little less top end
Echoes fading in, repeating longer, and a little more drive
Unison voices detuning, spreading out, and a little less level
Chorus copies fading in, drifting further, and a little more top end
C5M.15.why: Width, movement and brightness reinforce each other, so the sound seems to open out.

C5M.15.q: Shimmer's chorus copies have faded in, but they hardly drift. Which slot's amount do you raise?
options: The Chorus mix slot
The EQ high slot
The Chorus depth slot
None: drifting cannot be put on a macro
C5M.15.why: Chorus depth is the slot that makes the copies drift further.

C5M.15.q: How strong is each of the three Shimmer changes when heard alone?
options: None is dramatic alone; together they are heard as one change
Each is dramatic alone; together they cancel out
Only the chorus is heard; the others do nothing
Each is silent alone; all three are needed for any sound
C5M.15.why: Several gentle effect moves add up and are heard as a single change.

C5M.15.q: Why keep the Shimmer macro's amounts moderate?
options: A macro with large amounts stops working halfway up
A macro that goes too far never gets turned right up
Moderate amounts make the three changes easy to tell apart
Large amounts would make the sound narrower at the top
C5M.15.why: Moderate amounts keep the whole of the macro's travel usable.

C5M.16.q: What does a larger fall in pitch do to a kick drum?
options: Gives it a sharper knock at the front
Makes it ring on for longer
Gives it a softer, rounder thud
Makes it lower in pitch all the way through
C5M.16.why: A kick's hardness is partly the size of its pitch fall: a bigger fall, a sharper knock.

C5M.16.q: Why does distortion help a kick on speakers that cannot reproduce its lowest note?
options: It makes the lowest note itself much louder
It adds harmonics, and those can still be heard
It removes the lowest note so nothing is missing
It makes the pitch fall happen more slowly
C5M.16.why: Distortion adds harmonics, so the drum is heard even where its lowest note is not.

C5M.16.q: Slot 1 of the Knock macro goes to Env 2 amount. What does that show about macros?
options: A macro can only ever be sent to an envelope's settings
An envelope can turn a macro up and down for you
A macro takes the place of the envelope
A macro can move an envelope's amount as well as a knob
C5M.16.why: A macro's destination can be how strongly an envelope acts, not only a knob of the sound.

C5M.16.q: Your kick carries on small speakers, but its front is too soft. Which slot's amount do you raise?
options: The Distortion drive slot, for a larger pitch fall
The Distortion drive slot, for fewer harmonics
The Env 2 amount slot, for a larger pitch fall
The Env 2 amount slot, for a smaller pitch fall
C5M.16.why: A larger fall in pitch gives a sharper knock, and the Env 2 amount slot sets that fall.

C5M.C.q: A macro changes three things at once. How many settings do you have to match in a round?
options: One: the macro's position
Three: one for each slot
Two: the first and last slots
Four: the macro and each slot
C5M.C.why: A macro position is one number, even when it changes three things.

C5M.C.q: A macro moves several things at once. Which should you listen to when matching?
options: Always the first slot's change
Always the quietest change
Whichever change you hear most clearly
All of them equally, every time
C5M.C.why: There is more to listen to than with one knob, so use the change you find easiest to judge.

C5M.C.q: Where on a crossfade macro is it hardest to hear the exact position?
options: At zero
Halfway
Fully up
Just above zero
C5M.C.why: Halfway on a crossfade is the hardest place to hear exactly.
